Sacred Biker Ground by Edge

Leave a Comment / Event Coverage, Free Departments / October 7, 2026

Sacred Biker Ground by Edge

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:17
Instaread

It’s September and the Smoke Out bike rally in Salisbury, NC just ended.  Three bikers chose to have their final remains interned at the event.  One family gathered at the entrance and spread the ashes of their loved one.  One biker removed his rear wheel, took off his tire and respectfully transferred the ashes of his biker brother to the inside of the tire.  Eventually, after a long smokey burnout, the tire popped and the crowd cheered, one final time, for the recently deceased.  I would also like my remains scattered at the Smoke Out when I go, however, I don’t want to be cremated so we may have a few issues.  

Back in the day, Indian Larry married the first couple at the Smoke Out.  Since then, almost every event has had a wedding or two.  Why would anybody choose this as a final resting spot?  Why do people choose the event for their wedding?

Chris Callen took the reins of the event five years, and he tends to use the term “steward” as opposed to “owner.”  I have often heard Chris comment that the Smoke Out is “sacred ground” for the bike culture.  He talks about the gathering with reverence and its influence during his development in the chopper life.  Scores of famous builders cut their teeth at the event and just last night I watched a video where Billy Lane did a 20-year look-back about the first Biker Build-Off.  To me, Billy is so talented and industrious he was always going to be a success, but he looks back at this Build Off / Smoke Out experience as a pivotal point.

It connects deeply with me, because my years have been planned around the event too.  Only recently I have begun to understand how many of us have this feeling.  Chris understood this well before I figured it out.  When you are part of the Smoke Out your year revolves around it.  Not just what am I building to ride there.  The Smoke Out faithful do not just show up to be entertained like so many events.  They show up to be part of the event.  They bring questionable ideas and make questionable decisions.  

My new job seems to be to walk around the event and have people tell me their stories and they are wild.  Maybe next year, we will start recording some of these stories, but the bottom line is most of them are about the entertainment they brought with them.  I recently heard a famous builder, who has attended all the major events for years, say that the Smoke Out is the last truly authentic rally in the United States. 

Is the Smoke Out the last bastion of pure freedom and fun?  Or can we support other rallies by stepping outside of our comfort zone and making questionable choices?  If one of your biker buddies leaves a bike event and tells you that… day old chili on a $9 hot dog was questionable choice, tell them to try harder.  

When you do find that sacred ground of pure freedom, sketchy decisions and family reunion, don’t let it go.  Get married there, make it part of your life.  Support it.  Ride free. 

—-Edge

Tales from the pits: Cedar Lake arena

Leave a Comment / Cultural Interest, Free Departments / October 5, 2026

On Thursday night we left after school to head to Cedar Lake. Friday morning, it was open practice for kids and at night it was open practice for adults. I rode from 9 am to 9pm. Friday night I had to flip my rear tire (DT4). At nine o’clock there was a hot dog eating contest. Everyone from D16 and D23 that camped were there. Our district referee and my friend’s dad participated. It was fun. 

Saturday, in heats I took all firsts. The track felt great but I had to mess around with my tires before mains because my rear tire (DT4) was down to the wire. My mom and I took my front DT4 off and put in on the rear. Adam Schmidt from the Flying Dutchmen gave me 4 old Maxxis tires so we put one of those on the front. 

In mains I took 2nd in open youth and 3rd in super mini. I was all over track so my mom checked my tire pressure and set it to 12. In 85 I took First which put me in the running for our district championship. After the races, we changed my rear tire to a Maxxis because that one was bald too. In total we did 4 tire changes. 

Sunday, I only went out for practice twice because I didn’t want to burn through my tires. In heats, I took two firsts and a second because my friend crashed which caused a staggered restart and the lights were messed up for the restart. In mains I took all firsts and was able to get enough points to win D16 championship for 85 and open youth. I gave my first-place trophies to a kid that try’s really hard to get on podium but can’t. 

Ryan Ortin (11 years old)

The 2026 ADV Cannonball Rally

Leave a Comment / Bikernet Daily News Bites, Free Departments / October 3, 2026

108 signed up.
75 started.
64 reached the Pacific.
Sean Ross wins the 2026 ADV Cannonball Rally by only 14 points after eight days, one continent and no sweep truck.

The 2026 ADV Cannonball Rally left Plymouth Rock, Massachusetts on September 16 and finished in Monterey, California on September 23. In between were eight days, eight overnight stops, 100 GPS checkpoints and no support crew for anyone.

The rally sold out and kept a waitlist. In all, 108 riders signed up, 75 took the start and 64 reached Monterey. They came from 26 US states, Canada, Norway and England. When scoring closed, Sean Ross of North Carolina had won by only 14 points, on a BMW R1250GSA wearing the number 3.

The winner, and the Steak Knives
Sean Ross finished with 1,122 points. He took the first to arrive bonus on Day 1 and Day 3, missed only four checkpoints in eight days, and stamped the Monterey finish line at 4:03 PM on the last afternoon, 57 minutes before scoring closed.

He won this rally the way it is meant to be won. He leaned on what he learned in 2025. He brought a motorcycle he trusted. He was consistently quick, he made good navigation choices and he never stopped moving. There were no wheelies down the highway and no hooligan heroics. It was real skill on and off the road, technical preparation and navigation, with a relentlessly positive attitude on top.

This rally has one winner. Second place gets the Steak Knives, and nobody else is ranked. This year the Steak Knives went to Josh Skidmore of Utah, on 1,108 points. He and Sean rode much of the final day within seconds of each other. Then a navigation error in the California coastal hills cost Josh the afternoon. He missed three ten point checkpoints, the finish line among them, and any two would have won him the rally. He rode in after the cutoff knowing exactly what had happened, and he could not have been cooler about it.

The final day was complicated for everyone. A fire in those same hills put at least one checkpoint out of reach.
